paras: The threatened tarring and lynching of Israel A. Beverlin took place at the railroad depot in Grafton, West Virginia, in early November 1888, when a crowd threatened him as he shipped his dead wife's body to Ohio. No one acted on the threats, which, according to the local paper, only awaited a leader. The Grafton press, whose accounts were reprinted in Morgantown and Wheeling, blamed Beverlin for his wife's death and kept urging that he be driven out.

Beverlin had lived in Grafton for about 25 years and belonged to the Baptist church, according to the Grafton Eagle, which had attacked him in its columns for four years. The paper said he had married his wife, a former milliner from Athens, Ohio, in 1885, and that trouble began after she found letters to him from Mary Dean of Macomb, Ohio. In June 1888, by the Eagle's account, he sold the furniture, drove his wife from the house, and left for Ohio, while she took refuge with Charles W. Good and sued for divorce and for damages against Dean.

By 3 November a Grafton paper reported that Mrs. Beverlin had recently given birth and lay "at the point of death" at Good's boarding house. The Eagle-Sentinel charged that Beverlin, back in town, called her unchaste on the streets, that the news left her delirious, and that he never visited her as she died.

After her death Beverlin took charge of the body and on a Saturday morning shipped it to Seneca, Ohio, riding on the same train. A crowd gathered on the depot platform, where "threats of tar and feathers and lynching were freely made," but no one stepped forward to lead it. Beverlin left unharmed, and no arrests are reported.

Beverlin went to McComb, Ohio, where a local paper reprinted the Grafton charges and proposed that a committee of citizens order him to leave, with tar and feathers and "a stout hickory rail" if he refused. The Grafton Eagle answered that its own town tolerated him, asked whether Grafton had "any grit," and declared that "Beverlin must go." No later report of violence against him was found.

All of the coverage came from the white press of West Virginia and drew on the Grafton papers. The Grafton Eagle called Beverlin a "monster in human form" and said that its people "will not tolerate the presence of this scoundrel," language the Eagle-Sentinel repeated in describing the depot crowd. The Wheeling Register ran the depot account on 12 November under the headline "Wanted to Tar and Feather Him" in a column of state news, adding only that Grafton had come "within one" of doing it.

The Morgantown New Dominion reprinted the Eagle's long attack on 10 November and on 1 December ran the Ohio and Grafton calls for tar and feathers under the line that "the way of the transgressor is hard." None of these papers questioned the crowd's threats, and none stated Beverlin's race.

The Eagle-Sentinel, as quoted in Wheeling, dated the birth of the child to "the 15th inst.," which cannot be squared with the 3 November report of a recent birth or the Eagle's statement that the infant was scarcely two weeks old.

reader.title: Threatened tarring and lynching of Israel A. Beverlin
bases: A crowd at the Grafton depot threatened tar and feathers and lynching against Beverlin, but no one acted, and the papers later only urged that he be driven out (A3, A5).

No one was killed or hurt: a crowd at the depot made threats of tar and feathers and lynching that 'only awaited a leadership', and no act followed (A3). The threats came in response to press charges that Beverlin's treatment of his wife caused her death (A2, A3).

The depot threats appear only in the Wheeling Register's quotation of the Grafton Eagle-Sentinel (A3); the New Dominion's reprints of the Grafton Eagle give the background and later calls to drive him out but not the depot scene (A2, A5).

accounts.label: Grafton Eagle-Sentinel (via Wheeling Register)
accounts.gist: After his wife's death Beverlin shipped her body to Seneca, Ohio, and a crowd on the depot platform freely threatened tar and feathers and lynching, lacking only a leader.

accounts.label: Grafton Eagle (via New Dominion)
accounts.gist: A long indictment of Beverlin's conduct toward his wife and an earlier partner, ending with the claim that the town would not tolerate him; a later item urged that he be driven out.

accounts.label: McComb, Ohio, Herald (via New Dominion)
accounts.gist: If the West Virginia account was true, a committee of citizens should order Beverlin to leave McComb, with tar and feathers and a rail if he refused.

framing.detail: The Grafton papers called Beverlin a 'monster in human form' and the 'creature Beverlin', regretted that the crowd lacked a leader, and openly urged tar and feathers and a rail.
The Wheeling Register ran the Eagle-Sentinel's account without comment under 'WANTED TO TAR AND FEATHER HIM' in a state news column.

versions.value: 'on the 15th inst.' per the Eagle-Sentinel as quoted in the Wheeling Register of 12 November
Already 'recently' born by 3 November; the infant 'scarce two weeks old' when the mother died

conflicts.note: A birth on 15 November cannot precede reports of 3 and 12 November; 'inst.' is likely an error in the quoted paper or its reprint, which would place the birth in October.

record_check.dossier: A threatened tarring and lynching by a depot crowd; no one was harmed (intimidation, lynching stage 'threatened').
Accused by the Grafton press of causing his wife's death by deserting, slandering and mistreating her; no criminal charge reported.
His alleged 'outrageous and inhuman treatment' of his wife, which the press said caused her death.

record_check.dossier: Correct, but it omits the cause (the wife's death) and the later calls in Grafton and McComb, Ohio, to drive him out with tar and feathers.
Four relevant items in two papers (Wheeling Register; The New Dominion, Morgantown, three times), 3 November to 1 December 1888.
